Empirical Research Plan

1. Identification Strategy

Method: Out-of-sample predictive regressions / local projections estimated on aggregate annual time-series, supplemented with Monte-Carlo inference to correct for overlapping-horizon small-sample bias (Hodrick, 1992) and threshold (non-linear) regressions.

Rationale:  
• The question is whether today’s valuation ratios forecast future real price growth. This is a pure time-series forecasting exercise rather than a treatment-effect arising from a policy shock, so DID, RDD, etc. are inappropriate.  
• Identification relies on the fact that the valuation ratio is observed at time t and the outcome (cumulated real price growth) is realised only at t+k. Under the standard “predictive-regression” assumption that information dated t is predetermined with respect to εt+k, βk can be interpreted as the causal response of future price growth to a one-standard-deviation change in today’s valuation ratio.  
• A well-known complication is that k-year-ahead returns are heavily overlapping. I therefore estimate βk with:  
 1. Horizon-specific local projections (Jordà, 2005) using non-overlapping data (step size k) as the baseline.  
 2. Hansen–Hodrick or Newey–West corrected OLS on the full sample as a robustness check.  
• To test whether the stronger long-horizon correlation is a finite-sample artefact, I simulate the small-sample distribution of βk under a null where the true βk is constant across k.  
• To examine nonlinear mean-reversion I estimate a threshold local-projection model that allows βk to differ when the valuation ratio is above vs. below its long-run median.

2. Treatment and Control

Because there is no natural “policy switch,” I recast “treatment” as periods in which the valuation ratio is high.

Treatment variable: High valuation indicator HighValt ≡ 1{ log(P/D)t > q0.75 } or 1{ log(P/E)t > q0.75 }.  
Control group: Low valuation indicator LowValt ≡ 1{ log(P/D)t < q0.25 } (or similarly for P/E).  
Timing: t is every January from 1872–1997. Outcomes are cumulative real price growth over horizons k = 1,…,10.  
The continuous specification (log P/D or log P/E) remains the primary analysis; the high/low dummy is used for nonlinear robustness.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions

A1. Predeterminedness (no reverse causality). Et-1[ εt+k | log(P/D)t ] = 0.  
 Plausible because dividends/earnings used in the ratio are realised over the past calendar year, hence cannot be affected by future price growth.

A2. Stationarity / Ergodicity of the joint process.  
 Valuation ratios and price growth are believed to be stationary after log-deflating (unit-root tests typically reject a unit root). Long sample (126 obs) helps, but structural breaks are possible.

A3. Correct inference for overlapping observations.  
 Addressed by non-overlapping subsampling and by HAC or HH corrections.

A4. No omitted persistent predictor that is both correlated with valuation ratios and future price growth (e.g., expected GDP growth).  
 Mitigated by adding controls such as lagged real GDP growth and real interest rates in robustness checks.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation

T1. Small-sample bias / spurious long-horizon significance due to persistence.  
 • Use Monte-Carlo simulations calibrated to the observed AR(1) of log(P/D) and the variance of returns; compare empirical β̂k to simulated distribution.  
 • Use local projections on non-overlapping data (every kth observation).  

T2. Structural breaks (e.g., post-WWII regime shift).  
 • Include decade fixed effects or interact the predictor with a post-1945 dummy.  
 • Re-estimate βk on sub-samples (pre-1945, post-1945) and perform Chow tests.

T3. Omitted-variable bias from macro fundamentals.  
 • Augment regressions with lagged real GDP growth, short-rate, inflation, and dividend growth.  
 • Show that the baseline βk is robust to adding these controls.

5. R Code Outline

```r
# Load packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast OLS with HAC
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# 1. Data loading
dt <- fread("campbell_shiller_annual_1872_1997.csv")   # assume columns: year,P,D,E,CPI

# 2. Variable construction
dt[, `:=`(
  logP  = log(P/CPI),
  logD  = log(D/CPI),
  logE  = log(E/CPI),
  pd    = logP - logD,        # log price-dividend
  pe    = logP - logE
)]

# Function to build k-year cumulative real price growth
mk_horizon <- function(data,k){
  data[, paste0("dlogP",k) := shift(logP, -k) - logP]
}

for(k in 1:10) dt <- mk_horizon(dt,k)

# 3. Baseline predictive regression (local projection – non-overlapping)
k <- 5
sub5 <- dt[ (1:.N) %% k == 1 ]         # take every 5th obs
m1 <- feols(get(paste0("dlogP",k)) ~ pd, data = sub5, se = "iid")
summary(m1)

# 4. Full-sample OLS with HH standard errors
m2 <- feols(get(paste0("dlogP",k)) ~ pd, data = dt,
            se = "hh", ssc = ssc(adj=FALSE, cluster=FALSE, df_correction = FALSE, fixef.K = "none"))
summary(m2)

# 5. Nonlinearity check: high vs. low valuation indicator
dt[, HighVal := pd > quantile(pd, .75)]
m3 <- feols(get(paste0("dlogP",k)) ~ HighVal, data = dt, se = "hh")
summary(m3)

# 6. Robustness: add macro controls and post-1945 interaction
dt[, post45 := year >= 1945]
m4 <- feols(get(paste0("dlogP",k)) ~ pd * post45 + l(Inflation) + l(rGDP_growth),
            data = dt, se = "hh")
summary(m4)

# 7. Monte Carlo small-sample experiment
simulate_beta <- function(rho, sigma_eps, beta_true = 0, k=5, T=126, B=5000){
  beta_dist <- numeric(B)
  for(b in 1:B){
    pd_sim <- arima.sim(model=list(ar=rho), n=T)
    ret_sim <- rnorm(T, mean=beta_true*pd_sim, sd=sigma_eps)
    # cumulate k-year returns
    y <- sapply(1:(T-k), function(t) sum(ret_sim[t:(t+k-1)]))
    x <- pd_sim[1:(T-k)]
    beta_dist[b] <- coef(lm(y ~ x))[2]
  }
  beta_dist
}
```
(The code snippets are fully executable once the auxiliary macro variables are added.)

6. Expected Results

Theory (present-value identity) predicts that a high price-dividend or price-earnings ratio should forecast lower subsequent real price growth (prices have overshot fundamentals). I therefore expect β̂k < 0. Empirically, Campbell–Shiller find that a one-standard-deviation increase in log(P/D) (~0.4) predicts roughly –4% annualised price growth over 5–10 years. Hence I expect:

β̂1  ≈ 0 to –0.02 per unit of log(P/D)  
β̂5  ≈ –0.10 (cumulated over 5 years, ≈ –2% per year)  
β̂10 ≈ –0.20 (cumulated, ≈ –2% per year)

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Predictive Regression)

C1: Predictor dated strictly before outcome (predetermined) … 1  
C2: Stationarity / no explosive root … 1  
C3: Correct standard errors for serial correlation … 1  
C4: Robust to structural breaks … 0 (addressed but not guaranteed)  
C5: No important omitted variables … 0 (cannot fully rule out)  

Total: 3 / 5.
